meta.name: Adaptive developmental screening dataset
meta.disclaimer: Screening aid only, not a diagnostic tool. Base rates, likelihood ratios and age exponents are estimates for model v1 and must be calibrated against confirmed clinical outcomes before percentages are treated as true probabilities.
meta.question_polarity: Every question is phrased so that 'Yes' means the concern is present.
meta.provenance: Questions, age windows, condition links and sources from the Early Development Map evidence base (94 behaviours, 44 references), written in original wording. Numbers, follow-ups and rules added for the adaptive engine.

conditions.name: Autism spectrum disorder
conditions.dx_age_text: Reliable from ~18–24 m; signs from 6–12 m
conditions.base_rate_note: India: 1.0% of children aged 2-9 years (INCLEN, Arora et al. PLoS Med 2018;15(7):e1002615). Omli screens Indian children, so the Indian rate is used. Was 3% (CDC ADDM 2025, US) in Saathi.
conditions.note: DSM-5-TR: persistent social-communication deficits (A1–A3) + ≥2 restricted/repetitive behaviors (B1–B4), early onset.
conditions.refer: Developmental pediatrician / child psychologist. M-CHAT-R/F (16–30 m), ADOS-2, plus audiology. Genetic testing (microarray, FMR1) after diagnosis.

conditions.name: Late talker (expressive language delay)
conditions.base_rate_note: About 10–15% of 2-year-olds (Rescorla; Zubrick et al. 2007).
conditions.note: <50 words or no word combinations at 24 m with otherwise typical development. ~50–70% catch up by 3–4 y; the rest go on to DLD.
conditions.refer: Speech-language pathologist (SLP) language evaluation; hearing test. Recheck at 30 and 36 m; if still behind after ~4 y → assess for DLD.

conditions.name: Developmental language disorder
conditions.base_rate_note: Norbury et al. 2016: about 7.6% at school entry.
conditions.note: Language problems persisting past ~4–5 y not explained by hearing loss, ASD, ID. Formerly SLI. ~7% prevalence.
conditions.refer: SLP standardized language assessment (e.g. CELF Preschool), hearing test, nonverbal cognitive screen.

conditions.name: Speech sound disorder (articulation/phonological)
conditions.base_rate_note: ASHA: about 8–9% of young children.
conditions.note: Errors in producing sounds beyond age expectations; intelligibility below norms.
conditions.refer: SLP speech-sound assessment (articulation + phonology), oral-motor exam, hearing test.

conditions.name: Childhood apraxia of speech
conditions.base_rate_note: Shriberg et al.: about 1–2 per 1,000 children.
conditions.note: Motor-planning disorder of speech: inconsistent errors, disrupted coarticulation, inappropriate prosody (ASHA 2007).
conditions.refer: SLP experienced in motor speech: speech sample, repeated-word inconsistency testing, oral-motor exam.

conditions.name: Stuttering (childhood-onset fluency disorder)
conditions.base_rate_note: Yairi & Ambrose: about 5% of children go through a stuttering phase.
conditions.note: Sound/syllable repetitions, prolongations, blocks. ~75–80% recover spontaneously.
conditions.refer: SLP fluency evaluation (sooner if tension, family history, or >6 months).

conditions.name: Social (pragmatic) communication disorder
conditions.base_rate_note: Little population data; conservative estimate.
conditions.note: Pragmatic deficits WITHOUT restricted/repetitive behaviors (if RRBs present → ASD).
conditions.refer: SLP pragmatic language assessment; rule out ASD (check for restricted/repetitive behaviors).

conditions.name: Hearing loss
conditions.dx_age_text: Screen by 1 m, dx by 3 m, intervene by 6 m (JCIH 1-3-6)
conditions.base_rate_note: Permanent hearing loss about 1–3 per 1,000 at birth, rising in early childhood; includes persistent conductive loss. Estimate.
conditions.note: Always rule out with audiology before any language/ASD diagnosis.
conditions.refer: Audiology now: OAE / ABR (infants), behavioral audiometry (toddlers), tympanometry for glue ear. Do this before any other diagnosis.

conditions.name: Global developmental delay / intellectual disability
conditions.base_rate_note: About 1–3% of children under 5 (Shevell et al.).
conditions.note: Delay in ≥2 domains. Development is delayed but usually even across domains (vs ASD's uneven, social-specific profile).
conditions.refer: Developmental pediatrician; developmental assessment (e.g. Bayley-4), chromosomal microarray, FMR1, metabolic work-up as indicated.

conditions.name: Motor delay / cerebral palsy / hypotonia
conditions.base_rate_note: Cerebral palsy about 2–3 per 1,000 plus other significant motor delay and hypotonia. Estimate.
conditions.note: Neuromotor disorders; early motor red flags overlap with GDD.
conditions.refer: Pediatric neurologist + physiotherapist; HINE / GMA in infancy for cerebral palsy risk.

conditions.name: Developmental coordination disorder (dyspraxia)
conditions.base_rate_note: DSM-5-TR: 5–6% of school-age children.
conditions.note: Motor coordination well below age; interferes with daily life; not due to CP/ID.
conditions.refer: Occupational therapist / physio: motor assessment (MABC-2); rule out neurological causes.

conditions.name: ADHD
conditions.base_rate_note: Polanczyk et al. meta-analyses: about 5% of children; preschool estimates vary.
conditions.note: Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, ≥6 months, ≥2 settings, beyond developmental level. Preschool activity levels overlap heavily with typical.
conditions.refer: Pediatrician / child psychiatrist: rating scales from parent + teacher (e.g. Vanderbilt, Conners EC). Under 4 y: parent-training, monitor.

conditions.name: Sensory processing differences
conditions.base_rate_note: Not a DSM diagnosis; reported 5–16%. Conservative estimate.
conditions.note: Over-/under-responsivity or seeking. Not a stand-alone DSM diagnosis; sensory reactivity is an ASD criterion (B4). Often co-occurs with ADHD, anxiety.
conditions.refer: Occupational therapist (sensory profile). Screen for ASD, ADHD, anxiety since sensory issues are rarely isolated.

conditions.name: Anxiety disorders
conditions.base_rate_note: Preschool anxiety disorders about 2–9% (Egger & Angold).
conditions.note: Separation anxiety, specific phobias, generalized; behavioral inhibition in toddlers is a risk marker.
conditions.refer: Child psychologist; parent-led CBT approaches for preschoolers.

conditions.name: Selective mutism
conditions.dx_age_text: Onset usually <5 y; seen at school entry
conditions.base_rate_note: About 0.5–1% of young children.
conditions.note: Consistent failure to speak in specific settings (school) despite speaking elsewhere, ≥1 month (not first month of school).
conditions.refer: Child psychologist + SLP (screen language, since many children with SM also have speech/language difficulty).

conditions.name: Tic disorders / Tourette
conditions.base_rate_note: Tourette about 0.3–1%; transient tics much more common. Estimate for tics worth reviewing.
conditions.note: Sudden, rapid, recurrent non-rhythmic movements/vocalizations; wax and wane.
conditions.refer: Pediatrician / pediatric neurologist; screen for ADHD, OCD, anxiety.

conditions.name: Rett syndrome
conditions.base_rate_note: About 1 in 10,000 girls.
conditions.note: Normal-looking early period → loss of purposeful hand use and speech, hand stereotypies, gait problems.
conditions.refer: URGENT pediatric neurologist; MECP2 genetic testing; head-circumference chart.

conditions.name: Fragile X syndrome
conditions.base_rate_note: About 1 in 4,000 males and 1 in 8,000 females.
conditions.note: Most common inherited cause of ID; ~30–50% of males meet ASD criteria. AAP recommends FMR1 testing for ASD/GDD.
conditions.refer: FMR1 DNA test (recommended for every child with ASD or GDD); genetic counselling for family.

conditions.name: Landau-Kleffner syndrome
conditions.base_rate_note: Very rare.
conditions.note: Acquired epileptic aphasia: loss of language comprehension (verbal auditory agnosia) after normal development; EEG abnormal in sleep.
conditions.refer: URGENT pediatric neurologist: sleep EEG; audiology to exclude hearing loss.

conditions.name: Dyslexia risk (reading disorder precursors)
conditions.dx_age_text: Formal dx ≥6–7 y; risk visible 4–5 y
conditions.base_rate_note: About 5–10% of children.
conditions.note: Phonological awareness, letter knowledge, rapid naming, family history, preschool language problems.
conditions.refer: Phonological awareness + letter-knowledge screen at 5 y; early literacy intervention; SLP if language weak.

conditions.name: Hyperlexia
conditions.base_rate_note: Rare; estimate.
conditions.note: Precocious word decoding well above comprehension; most often seen with ASD.
conditions.refer: SLP language comprehension assessment and ASD evaluation.

prior_modifiers.label: Family history of speech, language or reading difficulty
Family history of stuttering or tics

eligibility.rule: past if age > dx_max_m; hidden if age < dx_min_m - 12; watch if age < dx_min_m; otherwise ok

age_lens.askable: not background AND window_start_m <= age <= window_end_m AND (typical_m is null OR age >= typical_m)
situation_rule: if direction < 0 and domain == CRS: history_item
elif direction > 0 and red_flag_m >= 6 and age >= 1.5 * red_flag_m: well_past_red_flag
elif red_flag_m is set and age >= red_flag_m: past_red_flag

damping.applies_to: Yes and No answers, counted separately for each direction
damping.formula: 0.8^(earlier same-direction answers for k in the same domain) * 0.93^(earlier same-direction answers for k overall)

branching.selection_score: sum over linked eligible k of weight_k * p_k(1-p_k) * (|ln LR+|*exp_present + |ln LR-|*exp_absent)
branching.follow_up_rule: After a Yes or Probably, the listed follow-up questions (if askable and unanswered) get the follow_up bonus for the next 4 answers. Follow-ups steer the adaptive score; they never force a question that isn't askable.

reason_text.first: Asked early for every child, because it changes what needs to happen first.

rules.when: Any is_urgent question answered Yes or Probably
rules.then: Interrupt with an urgent message; overall action becomes 'urgent' regardless of scores

rules.when: Any milestone question answered Yes when the child is at least 1.5 times its red-flag age (e.g. not sitting at 14 months)
rules.then: Overall action is at least 'refer', whatever the probabilities

rules.when: Any Yes-direction answer to a question linked to HL
rules.then: Add 'Get a hearing test first' to the next steps

rules.when: Condition eligibility is hidden or past
rules.then: Never show the condition and exclude it from question selection; watch-only conditions are labelled 'early signs, too young to confirm'

rules.when: Any RRB-domain question answered Yes or Probably
rules.then: Cap SPCD at 0.10 (by DSM-5-TR definition SPCD excludes restricted/repetitive behaviours; the pattern points to autism instead)

rules.when: 2 or more Yes/Probably answers to questions that are core autism signs (strength 3) in the SOC, PRE or PLAY domains
rules.then: Cap LT at 0.25 (late talker means otherwise typical development; the social signs point to autism or global delay instead)
Late talker becomes 'past'; persistent language concerns are scored under DLD
Report pattern strength and an action, never a diagnosis
Every result includes a recheck interval

actions.when: Any urgent red flag answered Yes or Probably
actions.title: See a doctor within the next few days

actions.when: Any ok-eligible condition with p >= 0.30, or the major_milestone_missed rule fires

questions.question: Does your child rarely look at your eyes when you talk or play together?
questions.clinical_name: Limited or declining eye contact
questions.typical: Looks at your face from birth; looks into your eyes during feeding, talking and play.
questions.differentiation: ASD: eye-looking declines from 2–6 m (Jones & Klin) and is poorly coordinated with gestures/voice. FXS & anxiety: child is interested in people but averts gaze (social anxiety), especially at greeting.

questions.question: Does your child rarely smile back at you or smile at you to get your attention?
questions.clinical_name: Few social smiles / warm, joyful expressions
questions.typical: Smiles back when you smile/talk (2 m); smiles to get your attention, chuckles (4 m); laughs (6 m).
questions.differentiation: In ASD, social smiling and directed facial expressions decline between 6 and 18 m after initially looking typical (Ozonoff 2010).

questions.question: When you call your child's name from behind (without them seeing you), do they often not turn to look?
questions.clinical_name: Does not respond to own name
questions.typical: Looks when you call their name (9 m), consistently by 12 m.
questions.differentiation: Hearing loss: no response to many sounds. ASD: responds to non-social sounds (TV jingle, chip packet) but not to name/voice. ADHD (4 y+): absorbed in activity, responds on repeat.

questions.question: If you point at a toy across the room, does your child NOT look at it?
questions.clinical_name: Does not follow your point or gaze (response to joint attention)
questions.typical: Looks where you point or look by ~12 m; looks at familiar object when you name it (15 m).
questions.differentiation: One of the strongest early ASD discriminators (SACS, M-CHAT). In GDD it is delayed but appears in line with overall developmental level.

questions.question: Does your child NOT point with one finger to show you something interesting (e.g. an airplane in the sky)?
questions.clinical_name: No pointing to show interest (declarative pointing)
questions.typical: Points to ask for something (15 m); points to show you something interesting (18 m).
questions.differentiation: Late talkers and CAS usually point and gesture a lot to compensate for missing words; ASD children may only pull your hand or point to request, rarely to share.

questions.question: Does your child NOT bring things to show you just so you can see them (not for help)?
questions.clinical_name: Does not show or bring objects just to share
questions.typical: Shows you an object they like (15 m); brings things to show you.
questions.differentiation: Showing for sharing (not for help) is specifically reduced in ASD.

questions.question: When something exciting happens, does your child NOT look at you to share it?
questions.clinical_name: Little shared enjoyment / social referencing
questions.typical: Looks at your face to check your reaction in a new situation (24 m); shares excitement by looking at you and back.
questions.differentiation: Coordinating gaze + smile + sound toward a person is a core early ASD indicator (Wetherby 2004).

questions.question: Does your child take your hand and put it on things they want, without looking at you?
questions.clinical_name: Uses your hand as a tool / leads you without looking at you
questions.typical: Uses eye contact + gesture/words to request help.
questions.differentiation: Leading by the hand is not abnormal by itself; the red flag is doing it without looking at your face or combining it with gesture.

questions.question: Does your child seem uninterested in other children?
questions.clinical_name: Little interest in other children
questions.typical: Watches other children, copies them (15 m); plays next to and sometimes with them (30 m); joins them (3 y).
questions.differentiation: Anxious / selectively mute children are interested and watch peers but hang back; ASD children often show low interest.

questions.question: If someone is crying or hurt, does your child not seem to notice?
questions.clinical_name: Does not notice or respond to others' distress
questions.typical: Notices when others are hurt/upset (24 m); comforts others (4 y).
questions.differentiation: Theory-of-mind differences in ASD; in SPCD the issue is mostly in expressing/adapting, not noticing.

questions.question: Does your child struggle to play cooperatively with other children (taking turns, following game rules)?
questions.clinical_name: Difficulty joining, sharing and turn-taking in peer play
questions.typical: Asks to play with children (4 y); follows rules / takes turns in games (5 y).
questions.differentiation: ASD: doesn't understand social rules / one-sided play. ADHD: understands but can't wait, grabs, impulsive. DLD: follows less because of language load.

questions.question: Does your child seem to want to be with people but turn their face away or bite their hand when greeted?
questions.clinical_name: Wants contact but averts gaze, hand-biting when socially overwhelmed
questions.typical: Comfortable eye contact with familiar people after warm-up.
questions.differentiation: Classic Fragile X profile: social interest + hyperarousal/anxiety, gaze aversion at greeting, hand-biting/flapping, perseverative speech.

questions.question: Does your child NOT enjoy games like peek-a-boo or pat-a-cake?
questions.clinical_name: Does not enjoy back-and-forth social games (peek-a-boo, pat-a-cake)
questions.typical: Smiles/laughs at peek-a-boo (9 m); plays pat-a-cake (12 m).
questions.differentiation: Enjoying people-games (not just tickles) is one of the early social markers.

questions.question: Does your child NOT copy what you do (e.g. clapping, waving, making a face)?
questions.clinical_name: Does not imitate actions, sounds or facial expressions
questions.typical: Copies other children while playing (15 m); copies you doing chores (18 m).
questions.differentiation: CAS: imitates actions fine but struggles to imitate speech sounds/words. ASD: imitation broadly reduced (actions and sounds).

questions.question: Does your child rarely play with toys the usual way (e.g. rolling a car, feeding a doll)?
questions.clinical_name: Does not use toys/objects the way they are meant to be used
questions.typical: Tries to use things the right way: phone, cup, book (15 m); pushes toy car (18 m).
questions.differentiation: ASD: may mouth, spin, line up or look closely at toys instead. GDD: delayed but appropriate to mental age.

questions.question: Does your child NOT play pretend (talking on a toy phone, cooking pretend food, caring for a doll)?
questions.clinical_name: No pretend / symbolic play
questions.typical: Uses things to pretend, e.g. feeding a block to a doll (30 m); pretends to be something else (4 y).
questions.differentiation: Pretend play is reduced and less flexible in ASD; delayed in GDD; mildly reduced in DLD (language-dependent play).

questions.question: Does your child play the same way, in the same order, again and again, and get upset if you change it?
questions.clinical_name: Play is repetitive, scripted, same sequence every time
questions.typical: Play becomes more varied and flexible, often with stories and roles.
questions.differentiation: Re-enacting video scenes word-for-word, distress if someone changes the sequence → ASD.

questions.question: Is your baby very quiet, rarely making cooing sounds?
questions.clinical_name: Few vocal sounds / no cooing
questions.typical: Makes sounds other than crying (2 m); coos 'oooo/aahh', makes sounds back when you talk (4 m).
questions.differentiation: Very quiet infancy is reported retrospectively in CAS; low vocal frequency in ASD (Patten 2014).

questions.question: When you talk to your baby and pause, does your baby NOT 'answer' with sounds?
questions.clinical_name: No vocal turn-taking with caregiver
questions.typical: Takes turns making sounds with you (6 m).
questions.differentiation: Social direction of sounds (sounds aimed at a person) matters more than the amount of sound.

questions.question: By 9–12 months, does your baby NOT babble with sounds like 'baba', 'dada', 'mama'?
questions.clinical_name: No canonical babbling ('bababa', 'mamama')
questions.typical: Makes repeated consonant-vowel sounds like 'mamama', 'bababa' (9 m). Usual onset ~6–10 m.
questions.differentiation: Late canonical babbling (>10 m) predicts later speech/language disorder (Oller 1999). Deaf infants' babbling is delayed – classic hearing-loss sign. CAS: limited consonant/vowel repertoire.

questions.question: By 12 months, does your child NOT wave bye-bye or reach up to be picked up?
questions.clinical_name: No conventional gestures (waving, reaching arms up, nodding)
questions.typical: Lifts arms to be picked up (9 m); waves bye-bye (12 m); more gestures like blowing kiss, nodding (24 m).
questions.differentiation: AAN absolute indication: no gesturing by 12 m. Late talkers who gesture well have better outcomes (Thal 1992).

questions.question: When your child can't say a word, do they also NOT try to show you by pointing, gesturing or pulling you?
questions.clinical_name: Does not compensate for missing words with gestures, sounds or eye contact
questions.typical: Toddlers with few words still communicate a lot through gestures, sounds and looks.
questions.differentiation: KEY DIFFERENTIATOR: late talkers, CAS and hearing-loss kids usually compensate (gesture/point/mime); children with ASD communicate less overall, not just with words.

questions.question: Does your baby not startle at loud noises or not turn toward your voice?
questions.clinical_name: Does not react / turn to sounds
questions.typical: Reacts to loud sounds (2 m); turns head toward your voice (4 m).
questions.differentiation: Inconsistent response (ignores loud voice, notices a tiny favorite sound) points more to ASD than hearing loss — but always test hearing.

questions.question: Does your child often ask 'what?', want the TV loud, or understand better when looking at your face?
questions.clinical_name: Hearing-loss pattern: watches faces closely, wants TV loud, says 'huh?' often
questions.typical: Understands speech from another room or without seeing your face.
questions.differentiation: Recurrent ear infections / glue ear cause fluctuating hearing that can mimic delay or inattention.

questions.question: Does your child NOT seem to understand simple words like 'no', 'mama', 'ball'?
questions.clinical_name: Does not understand simple words ('no', names of familiar people/objects)
questions.typical: Understands 'no' (12 m); looks at familiar object when you name it (15 m).
questions.differentiation: Receptive delay alongside expressive delay is a worse prognostic sign for late talkers than expressive delay alone.

questions.question: If you say 'give me the cup' without pointing, does your child NOT do it?
questions.clinical_name: Does not follow simple one-step directions without gestures
questions.typical: Follows directions with gesture + words (15 m); one-step directions without gestures, e.g. 'give it to me' (18 m).
questions.differentiation: Test without pointing/looking — children rely on context cues.

questions.question: If you ask 'where's your nose?' or 'show me the dog' in a book, does your child NOT point?
questions.clinical_name: Does not point to pictures or body parts when named
questions.typical: Points to things in a book when you ask; points to at least two body parts (24 m).

questions.question: Does your child have trouble following two-step instructions like 'take your shoes and put them in the cupboard'?
questions.clinical_name: Difficulty with two-step instructions and 'wh-' questions
questions.typical: Follows two-step instructions (30 m); answers 'what is a coat for?' (4 y); answers questions about a story (5 y).
questions.differentiation: ADHD: understands when attending; repeat instruction once with attention → succeeds. DLD: still fails because of language load.

questions.question: Does your child struggle to understand words like 'under', 'behind', 'big/small' or 'yesterday'?
questions.clinical_name: Difficulty with concepts (in/on/under, big/little, colors, yesterday/tomorrow)
questions.typical: Knows a color (30 m); names a few colors (4 y); uses time words (5 y).

questions.question: By 16 months, does your child NOT say any real words?
questions.clinical_name: No single words
questions.typical: Says 'mama/dada' or special name (12 m); 1–2 more words (15 m); 3+ words (18 m).
questions.differentiation: AAN absolute indication: no single words by 16 m. Check: understanding, gestures, hearing.

questions.question: At 2 years, does your child say fewer than 50 words?
questions.clinical_name: Small vocabulary (<50 words at 24 m)
questions.typical: About 50 words at 30 m (CDC); typical 24-month-olds average 200–300.
questions.differentiation: Late-talker definition (Rescorla LDS). Risk of persisting to DLD higher with: poor comprehension, few gestures, family history, little babbling, no improvement by 30 m.

questions.question: By 2 years, does your child NOT put two words together on their own (not copying)?
questions.clinical_name: No spontaneous two-word phrases
questions.typical: Says at least two words together, e.g. 'more milk' (24 m); with an action word, 'doggie run' (30 m).
questions.differentiation: AAN absolute indication: no spontaneous (non-echoed) 2-word phrases by 24 m. Echoed or memorized phrases don't count.

questions.question: Does your child speak in short sentences and often leave out small grammar words (e.g. 'he go park')?
questions.clinical_name: Short, simple sentences; grammar errors (missing -s, -ed, is/are)
questions.typical: Asks who/what/where/why (3 y); sentences of 4+ words (4 y); mostly correct grammar by 5 y.
questions.differentiation: Persistent tense-marking errors ('he go', 'yesterday I play') are a hallmark of DLD in English; check norms for other languages/bilingual children (assess in all languages).

questions.question: Can your child NOT tell you something that happened today in a way you can follow?
questions.clinical_name: Difficulty telling about their day or retelling a story
questions.typical: Talks about one thing that happened in their day (4 y); tells a story with at least two events (5 y).
questions.differentiation: Narrative skill at 4–5 y is one of the best predictors of persisting language problems (CATALISE).

questions.question: Does your child often know what they want to say but can't find the word?
questions.clinical_name: Word-finding difficulty (lots of 'that thing', pauses, wrong-but-related words)
questions.typical: Retrieves known words quickly.

questions.question: Does your child often repeat what you say, or lines from cartoons/ads, instead of answering?
questions.clinical_name: Echolalia / scripting (repeating your words or lines from videos)
questions.typical: Some immediate echoing is normal while learning to talk, fading by ~30 m.
questions.differentiation: Persistent echolalia beyond ~30 m and using scripts in place of own speech → ASD (DSM B1). Echolalia can be functional — note its purpose for therapy planning.

questions.question: Does your child say 'you' when they mean 'I' (e.g. 'you want biscuit' for themselves)?
questions.clinical_name: Pronoun reversal / refers to self by name or 'you'
questions.typical: Uses 'I', 'me', 'we' (30 m).
questions.differentiation: 'You want juice' meaning 'I want juice' is linked to echolalia in ASD; general pronoun errors (her for she) are common in DLD.

questions.question: Does your child use words mostly to ask for things, and rarely to show or tell you things?
questions.clinical_name: Talks mainly to request, rarely to comment, share or ask
questions.typical: Uses words to comment ('look, doggie!'), share and ask questions, not only to get things.
questions.differentiation: Limited range of communicative functions is core ASD; a child with many words who only labels or requests is still a concern.

questions.question: Does your child use unusual words or phrases in a way that only family understands, or talk like an adult/TV?
questions.clinical_name: Unusual / idiosyncratic or adult-like (pedantic) language
questions.typical: Child-like phrasing appropriate to age.
questions.differentiation: Made-up words with private meaning, overly formal phrases, reciting facts.

questions.question: Is it hard to have a short back-and-forth chat with your child?
questions.clinical_name: Cannot keep a back-and-forth conversation going
questions.typical: 2 back-and-forth exchanges (3 y); more than 3 exchanges (5 y).
questions.differentiation: SM: converses normally at home. ADHD: interrupts/goes off topic. SPCD vs ASD: SPCD has no restricted/repetitive behaviors.

questions.question: Does your child talk at length about their own topic, or not understand jokes/hints that other kids their age get?
questions.clinical_name: Doesn't adapt talk to listener/situation; misses non-literal meaning; topic monologues
questions.typical: Changes behavior based on where they are (4 y); talks differently to babies vs adults.
questions.differentiation: DSM-5 SPCD criteria A1–A4. Usually not diagnosable until speech is sufficiently developed (~4–5 y).

questions.question: Does your child talk normally at home but not at all at school or with relatives/strangers for many weeks?
questions.clinical_name: Speaks freely at home but consistently silent at school or with outsiders
questions.typical: May be shy initially but speaks after warming up.
questions.differentiation: Must last >1 month (not the first month of school). Up to ~30–50% of SM children also have speech/language problems — assess both.

questions.question: Do people outside the family struggle to understand your child's speech?
questions.clinical_name: Hard for strangers to understand
questions.typical: Talks well enough for others to understand most of the time (3 y). Classic rule: ~50% at 2 y, 75% at 3 y, ~100% at 4 y to strangers (newer norms are slower).
questions.differentiation: Consistent pattern of errors → phonological SSD. Inconsistent errors + groping → CAS. Slurred/weak → dysarthria (motor).

questions.question: Does your child still swap or drop sounds a lot (e.g. 'tup' for 'cup', 'ca' for 'cat') after age 3½–4?
questions.clinical_name: Persistent sound-simplifying patterns (e.g. 'tat' for 'cat', dropping end sounds)
questions.typical: Most simplifying patterns (fronting, final-consonant deletion, stopping) fade by 3–4 y.
questions.differentiation: Phonological SSD (not motor articulation errors like a lisp) raises later literacy risk, especially with language problems.

questions.question: Does your child say the same word differently each time, or seem to struggle to get their mouth to make the word?
questions.clinical_name: Inconsistent errors on the same word; groping mouth; trouble with longer words
questions.typical: Errors, when present, are consistent and predictable.
questions.differentiation: ASHA's three CAS features: inconsistent errors on repeated productions, lengthened/disrupted transitions between sounds, inappropriate prosody. Child understands much more than they can say.

questions.question: Does your child repeat sounds ('m-m-mama'), stretch sounds ('sssssun') or get stuck with no sound coming out?
questions.clinical_name: Stuttering: sound/syllable repetitions ('b-b-ball'), prolongations, blocks
questions.typical: Whole-word or phrase repetitions ('I-I-I want') and 'um's are common and typical at 2–5 y.
questions.differentiation: Refer if: part-word repetitions/blocks, visible tension, eye-blinking/head movement, child is frustrated, lasts >6 months, onset after 3½ y, or family history of persistent stuttering.

questions.question: Does your child's voice sound unusual — flat, robotic, sing-song, or too loud/quiet?
questions.clinical_name: Unusual tone of voice — flat, sing-song, robotic, unusual pitch or loudness
questions.typical: Varied, natural melody of speech.
questions.differentiation: CAS: equal stress on syllables, choppy. HL: loud or nasal voice. ASD: sing-song, flat or unusual intonation, sometimes scripted voice.

questions.question: Does your child still drool a lot or have trouble with lip and tongue control after age 2?
questions.clinical_name: Persistent drooling / weak oral-motor control
questions.typical: Daytime drooling largely stops by ~24 m.
questions.differentiation: Dysarthria (weakness) differs from CAS (planning): weak lips/tongue at rest and during eating.

questions.question: Does your child often flap their hands, flick fingers near their eyes, rock or spin repeatedly?
questions.clinical_name: Repetitive body movements: hand-flapping, finger-flicking, rocking, spinning
questions.typical: Brief flapping when excited is common <2 y and alone is not a concern.
questions.differentiation: ASD-associated repetitive behaviors are elevated already at 12 m (Elison 2014). Stereotypies: rhythmic, early onset, prolonged, suppressible with distraction. Tics: sudden, brief, non-rhythmic, with urge, later onset.

questions.question: Has your child stopped using their hands to hold/play, and instead keeps wringing or clapping them at the middle of the body?
questions.clinical_name: Loss of purposeful hand use + midline hand-wringing/washing/clapping/mouthing
questions.typical: Increasingly skilled reaching, grasping and using hands.
questions.differentiation: Rett main criteria: partial/complete loss of purposeful hand skills and spoken language, gait abnormalities, stereotypic hand movements. Mostly girls. Urgent referral.

questions.question: Does your child spend a lot of time lining up toys, spinning wheels or opening/closing doors and get upset if interrupted?
questions.clinical_name: Lines up / sorts / spins objects; fixates on parts (wheels, doors, switches)
questions.typical: Explores and plays with whole toys in varied ways.
questions.differentiation: Many toddlers line things up; concern = intense, prolonged, preferred over other play, distress if disturbed.

questions.question: Does your child often look at things from the side of their eyes, or stare at ceiling fans, lights or spinning things?
questions.clinical_name: Unusual visual exploration: looks from corner of eye, stares at lights/fans, prefers moving patterns
questions.typical: Looks at objects and faces directly.
questions.differentiation: Atypical visual object exploration at 12 m (Ozonoff 2008); toddlers preferring geometric over social movies (Pierce 2011) are highly likely to have ASD.

questions.question: Does your child get very upset over small changes (a different route, cup, or order of doing things)?
questions.clinical_name: Insistence on sameness — extreme distress at small changes, rigid routines/rituals
questions.typical: Toddlers like routine but cope with changes with mild protest.
questions.differentiation: ASD (DSM B2): same route, same cup, same order, meltdown at small change. Anxiety: avoidance driven by fear, rather than need for sameness.

questions.question: Is your child intensely focused on one topic or object (e.g. letters, numbers, fans) and hard to draw away?
questions.clinical_name: Unusually intense or narrow interests (letters, numbers, logos, specific objects)
questions.typical: Interests are many and shift; favorites are common.
questions.differentiation: Intensity/focus that crowds out other play, or unusual objects of interest (DSM B3). Attachment to unusual objects (string, pens, a specific flashcard) rather than soft toys.

questions.question: Does your child have quick, sudden movements or noises (blinking, sniffing, throat clearing) that come and go?
questions.clinical_name: Tics: sudden repeated blinking, grimacing, shoulder shrug, sniffing, throat-clearing
questions.typical: Transient tics affect up to ~20% of children and often resolve.
questions.differentiation: Tourette = multiple motor + ≥1 vocal tic, >1 year, onset <18 y. ADHD co-occurs in ~50% of Tourette.

questions.question: Does your child get very upset by everyday sounds like a mixer, vacuum cleaner or hand dryer?
questions.clinical_name: Over-reacts to everyday sounds (covers ears for mixer, vacuum, pressure cooker)
questions.typical: May startle but settles quickly.
questions.differentiation: Sensory hyper/hypo-reactivity is DSM ASD criterion B4; sensory symptoms are markedly more common in ASD than in typical or DD groups (Ben-Sasson 2009).

questions.question: Does your child react very strongly to haircuts, nail-cutting, certain clothes or getting hands dirty?
questions.clinical_name: Tactile defensiveness: distress with haircuts, nail-cutting, clothing tags, messy hands, bathing
questions.typical: Mild dislike is common; tolerates with reassurance.

questions.question: Does your child seem not to notice when hurt, cold or dirty?
questions.clinical_name: Under-reacts: high pain tolerance, doesn't notice being touched, cold or wet
questions.typical: Reacts appropriately to pain and temperature.

questions.question: Does your child often smell, lick or chew non-food things, or crash into furniture/people on purpose?
questions.clinical_name: Sensory seeking: smells/licks non-food, mouths objects past 2 y, crashes, seeks deep pressure
questions.typical: Mouthing objects is normal in infancy and declines after ~18–24 m.
questions.differentiation: Persistent eating of non-food (pica) needs medical check (iron, lead).

questions.question: Can your child spin for a very long time without getting dizzy, OR are they very scared of swings and climbing?
questions.clinical_name: Seeks constant spinning/swinging without getting dizzy, or fears movement (feet off ground)
questions.typical: Enjoys movement play; gets dizzy after spinning.

questions.question: At 4–6 months, is your baby's head still wobbly or does it fall back when you pull them up to sit?
questions.clinical_name: Poor head control / head lag when pulled to sit
questions.typical: Holds head up on tummy (2 m); holds head steady when held (4 m).
questions.differentiation: Head lag at 6 m was associated with later ASD in high-risk infants (Flanagan 2012), but mainly signals motor/GDD.

questions.question: At 9 months, can your baby NOT sit on their own?
questions.clinical_name: Not sitting without support
questions.typical: Sits without support, gets into sitting by self (9 m).

questions.question: At 18 months, is your child NOT walking on their own?
questions.clinical_name: Not walking independently
questions.typical: Takes a few steps (15 m); walks without holding on (18 m).

questions.question: Does your child feel 'floppy' when you lift them or have unusually bendy joints?
questions.clinical_name: Floppy / low muscle tone, very flexible joints
questions.typical: Firm, age-appropriate tone.
questions.differentiation: Hypotonia + hyperextensible joints + social anxiety/ID → consider Fragile X testing.

questions.question: Does your baby always use only one hand and seem to ignore the other?
questions.clinical_name: Strong hand preference or one-sided movement before 18 m
questions.typical: Uses both hands; true hand preference usually appears after ~18–24 m.
questions.differentiation: Early handedness can indicate weakness on the other side (hemiplegic cerebral palsy).

questions.question: After age 3, does your child still walk on tiptoes most of the time?
questions.clinical_name: Persistent toe-walking
questions.typical: Toe-walking is common in new walkers; flat-foot walking by ~2–3 y.
questions.differentiation: Check for tight heel cords / spasticity (CP, muscular dystrophy).

questions.question: Does your child have a lot more trouble than peers with drawing, using a spoon, stacking blocks or buttons?
questions.clinical_name: Fine motor delay: pincer grasp, stacking, scribbling, crayon grip, buttons
questions.typical: Pincer grasp (12 m); scribbles (18 m); draws a circle when shown (3 y); holds crayon with fingers and thumb, draws person with 3 parts (4 y); buttons (5 y).

questions.question: Is your child much clumsier than other children their age (falls a lot, struggles to jump, hop or catch)?
questions.clinical_name: Clumsy: frequent falls, trouble with running, jumping, stairs, catching, hopping
questions.typical: Runs, kicks ball (24 m); jumps with both feet (30 m); catches large ball (4 y); hops on one foot (5 y).
questions.differentiation: ADHD clumsiness is often from impulsivity/inattention; DCD persists even when careful.

questions.question: Does your child take much longer than others to learn things like dressing, pedaling a tricycle, or using scissors?
questions.clinical_name: Trouble learning new motor sequences (dressing, pedaling, using tools)
questions.typical: Learns new motor tasks with a few tries.
questions.differentiation: Motor-planning (praxis) difficulties often co-occur with CAS.

questions.question: Was/is your baby unusually quiet and content to be alone for long periods, rarely calling for you?
questions.clinical_name: Unusually passive, quiet 'easy' baby; doesn't seek attention
questions.typical: Seeks attention by looking, moving, making sounds (4 m).
questions.differentiation: Passivity at 6 m and extreme distress reactions at 12 m reported in infants later diagnosed with ASD (Zwaigenbaum 2005).

questions.question: Is your baby very difficult to calm even when held, fed and comfortable?
questions.clinical_name: Very hard to soothe; extreme crying/irritability beyond infancy colic
questions.typical: Calms when spoken to or picked up (2 m).
questions.differentiation: Early regulatory problems (persistent crying, sleep, feeding) predict later behavior problems; non-specific alone.

questions.question: Does your child have very long or very frequent meltdowns, or hurt themselves (head-banging, biting) during them?
questions.clinical_name: Severe tantrums: very frequent, very long (>25 min), with self-harm or aggression
questions.typical: Tantrums peak at 18–48 m but are usually short (<5–10 min) and recover quickly.
questions.differentiation: Self-injury during tantrums, destruction, or many daily long tantrums are atypical (Belden 2008). In language-delayed children tantrums often decrease as communication improves.

questions.question: Does your child bang their head, bite or hit themselves when upset or bored?
questions.clinical_name: Self-injury: head banging, biting self, hitting self
questions.typical: Brief rhythmic head banging at bedtime can be benign in toddlers.

questions.question: Does your child stay frozen, silent or clingy for a long time in new places or with new people?
questions.clinical_name: Extreme shyness / behavioral inhibition with unfamiliar people and places
questions.typical: Stranger wariness 6–18 m (9 m: clingy around strangers is EXPECTED); warms up in minutes later on.
questions.differentiation: Note: stranger anxiety at 9 m is a typical milestone — absence can also be notable.

questions.question: Does your child get extremely upset when you leave, or have many strong fears that stop daily activities?
questions.clinical_name: Excessive fears, worry, separation distress beyond preschool age
questions.typical: Calms within 10 min after you leave (3 y).

questions.question: Once your child is focused on something, is it very hard to get their attention to something else?
questions.clinical_name: 'Sticky' attention — hard to shift from one thing to another
questions.typical: Shifts attention between people and objects easily.
questions.differentiation: Difficulty disengaging visual attention at 12 m in infants later diagnosed ASD (Zwaigenbaum 2005).

questions.question: Compared with children the same age, does your child have much more trouble staying with one activity?
questions.clinical_name: Very short attention span; flits between toys/activities
questions.typical: Pays attention for 5–10 minutes during activities (5 y).
questions.differentiation: Before 4 y high activity and short attention are typical; look for ≥6 months, ≥2 settings, clearly beyond peers.
questions.data_fix: Typical age corrected from 60 to 36 months; it was later than the red-flag age (48).

questions.question: Is your child 'driven by a motor' — running, climbing and unable to sit, much more than other kids?
questions.clinical_name: Constantly on the go; can't sit for meals, stories, circle time
questions.typical: Preschoolers are active but can sit for short, interesting tasks.

questions.question: Does your child act without thinking, like running into the road or grabbing things, much more than peers?
questions.clinical_name: Impulsive: runs into danger, can't wait turn, grabs, interrupts
questions.typical: Avoids danger, e.g. doesn't jump from tall heights (4 y).

questions.question: Does your child often seem not to hear you even when you speak to them directly?
questions.clinical_name: Seems not to listen when spoken to directly
questions.typical: Stops and attends when called by caregiver.
questions.differentiation: Classic confusable: rule out hearing (HL), comprehension (DLD), social orienting (ASD), seizure staring spells, before attributing to ADHD.

questions.question: Does your child eat fewer than ~15–20 foods, or only foods of one color, texture or brand?
questions.clinical_name: Extremely picky eating — very few foods, by color/texture/brand
questions.typical: Picky phases are common 2–5 y but diet stays reasonably varied.
questions.differentiation: Children with ASD have ~5× higher odds of feeding problems, mostly food selectivity (Sharp 2013).

questions.question: After 12 months, does your child still gag on or refuse anything that isn't smooth/pureed?
questions.clinical_name: Gags on lumpy/solid foods, trouble chewing past 12 m
questions.typical: Moves to mashed/finger foods by ~9–12 m; feeds self with fingers (15 m).

questions.question: Does your child regularly take over an hour to fall asleep or wake for long periods in the night?
questions.clinical_name: Persistent trouble falling/staying asleep
questions.typical: Most children sleep through the night most nights by 3 y.
questions.differentiation: Sleep problems worsen daytime behavior and attention — treat them before over-reading ADHD signs.

questions.question: Is your child far behind other kids their age in toilet training or dressing themselves?
questions.clinical_name: Delayed toilet training / self-care well behind peers
questions.typical: Most daytime toilet-trained by ~3–4 y; takes clothes off (30 m), puts some on (3 y).

questions.question: Does your child struggle to tell if words rhyme (cat–hat) or to hear the first sound in a word?
questions.clinical_name: Difficulty with rhymes, syllable clapping, first sounds of words
questions.typical: Says words from nursery rhymes (4 y); uses or recognizes simple rhymes like bat–cat (5 y).
questions.differentiation: Phonological awareness is among the strongest preschool predictors of reading (NELP 2008).

questions.question: By 5, does your child struggle to remember letter names/sounds even with practice?
questions.clinical_name: Trouble learning letter names/sounds and slow at naming familiar things
questions.typical: Names some letters when you point, writes some letters of name (5 y).
questions.differentiation: Slow rapid automatized naming (colors/objects) + weak letter knowledge + family history = high dyslexia risk.

questions.question: Did your child learn letters, numbers or to read words very early (before 3) but has trouble understanding conversation?
questions.clinical_name: Reads/recognizes letters, numbers or words very early, but understands little
questions.typical: Letter knowledge emerges around 4–5 y; comprehension keeps pace with decoding.
questions.differentiation: Precocious decoding with poor comprehension and language delay; strongly associated with ASD (Ostrolenk 2017).

questions.question: Has your child stopped saying words, babbling, waving or playing in ways they used to?
questions.clinical_name: Loss of words, babble or social skills they had before
questions.typical: Skills accumulate; brief plateaus happen but skills are not lost.
questions.differentiation: ANY loss at ANY age = urgent referral. ASD regression typically 15–24 m (~20–30% of ASD). Rett: 6–18 m with loss of hand use. LKS: 3–7 y, loss of comprehension. Also exclude seizures, metabolic, hearing.

questions.question: Has your child, who used to understand well, suddenly started acting as if they can't understand or hear words?
questions.clinical_name: Suddenly stops understanding speech ('acts deaf') after normal language
questions.typical: Comprehension keeps growing.
questions.differentiation: Hearing test normal + sleep EEG abnormal → LKS. Often with seizures (~70%), behavior change.

questions.question: (Clinician) Has head circumference crossed down percentile lines, or is it >97th percentile?
questions.clinical_name: Head growth slowing down (or unusually large head)
questions.typical: Head circumference follows its growth curve.
questions.differentiation: Clinician-measured. Deceleration between 3 m and 4 y supports Rett; macrocephaly occurs in a subgroup with ASD.

questions.question: Has your child had seizures, or brief staring spells where they can't be 'reached'?
questions.clinical_name: Seizures or staring spells
questions.typical: None.
questions.differentiation: Absence seizure staring can look like ADHD inattention; epilepsy rates are elevated in ASD.

questions.question: Does anyone in the family have autism, speech/language delay, reading difficulty, stuttering, ADHD or intellectual disability?
questions.clinical_name: Family history: sibling with autism; family speech/language, reading, stuttering, ADHD, intellectual disability
questions.background_note: Covered by the family-history step of the child profile.
questions.differentiation: Younger siblings of autistic children have ~19% ASD recurrence (Ozonoff 2011) → monitor closely from 6 m. Family history of dyslexia raises child's risk ~45%.

questions.question: Did your child fail a newborn hearing test, or have many ear infections?
questions.clinical_name: Failed newborn hearing screen, recurrent ear infections/glue ear, NICU stay
questions.typical: Passed newborn screen, few ear infections.
questions.differentiation: JCIH 1-3-6: screen by 1 m, diagnose by 3 m, intervene by 6 m. Refer for audiology before any speech/ASD evaluation.

questions.question: Was your child born before 37 weeks or very small, or did they need NICU care?
questions.clinical_name: Preterm birth / low birth weight / birth complications
questions.typical: Use corrected age for milestones until 24 m.
questions.background_note: Covered by the 'born' step of the child profile.
questions.differentiation: Always correct age for prematurity up to 2 y before judging milestones.

activities.title: Call their name from behind
activities.instructions: While your child is playing with something else, call their name once from a few feet behind them (don't touch them or wave anything in their view). Wait a few seconds, then try again if needed. Record 30-60 seconds of this.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether they turn or respond to their name without extra cues like touch or pointing.

activities.title: Point-and-look play
activities.instructions: Play with a toy your child likes for 2-3 minutes. Point at something across the room and say their name - see if they look where you point and look back at you.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether the child follows a point and shares attention with you.

activities.title: Pretend play sample
activities.instructions: Give your child a toy phone, empty cup, or doll and see what they do with it for a couple of minutes, without showing them first.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether they use the object to pretend (e.g. 'drinking' from the cup, 'talking' on the phone) rather than only lining it up or spinning it.

activities.title: Back-and-forth sound play
activities.instructions: Make a simple sound or coo at your baby, pause, and see if they make a sound back. Keep the 'conversation' going for a minute.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether sounds go back and forth between you, and the variety of sounds your baby makes.

activities.title: One-step instruction, no gestures
activities.instructions: Without pointing or looking at the object, ask your child to do one simple thing (e.g. 'bring me the ball', 'put the spoon in the cup'). Keep your hands still and face neutral.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether they can follow the instruction from words alone, without any gesture or cue.

activities.title: Natural talking sample
activities.instructions: Record about 2 minutes of your child talking naturally during play or a snack - no need to prompt them, just let them chatter.
activities.what_we_look_for: Roughly how many different words or word combinations they use on their own.

activities.title: Short back-and-forth chat
activities.instructions: Ask your child an open question about their day ('what did you do today?') and have a short back-and-forth conversation, about 2-3 exchanges.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether they stay on topic, take turns, and answer in a way that fits what you asked.

activities.title: Naming familiar objects
activities.instructions: Show your child 8-10 familiar objects or pictures one at a time and ask them to name each one.
activities.what_we_look_for: How clearly each word is said, and whether certain sounds are consistently left out or swapped.

activities.title: Relaxed talking sample
activities.instructions: Record 2 minutes of your child talking about something they enjoy, in a relaxed moment (not put on the spot).
activities.what_we_look_for: Repeated sounds or words, long blocks before speaking, or visible tension while talking.

activities.title: Free play with favourite toys
activities.instructions: Record 3 minutes of your child playing freely with a few toys they enjoy - don't direct the play, just let them choose.
activities.what_we_look_for: Repeated actions like lining up, spinning, or watching parts of objects, versus varied, flexible play.

activities.title: Everyday sounds and textures
activities.instructions: Over a normal day, record their reaction to a few ordinary things: a vacuum or blender, a scratchy or wet texture, a crowded or noisy moment.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether reactions seem much stronger or much weaker than other children their age.

activities.title: Moving around sample
activities.instructions: Record your child walking, running, climbing a step, or kicking a ball - whatever fits their age - for about a minute.
activities.what_we_look_for: Balance, coordination, and how their movements compare to other children their age.

activities.title: Small transition or limit
activities.instructions: Record a normal, mild moment of frustration you'd expect anyway - ending a favourite activity, or briefly saying no to something - and how your child responds and recovers.
activities.what_we_look_for: How big the reaction is and how long it takes them to settle afterwards.

activities.title: Short table activity
activities.instructions: Sit with your child for a short puzzle, drawing, or matching game and record about 5 minutes.
activities.what_we_look_for: How long they stay with the activity, how easily they're pulled away, and whether they wait their turn in back-and-forth parts.

activities.title: Mealtime with a new food
activities.instructions: Record part of a mealtime that includes one new or less-preferred food alongside familiar ones.
activities.what_we_look_for: How they react to the new food's texture, smell or appearance, and how it compares to familiar foods.

activities.title: Rhymes and letters
activities.instructions: Say a simple, familiar rhyme together and see if your child can join in or finish lines. Separately, point to 3-4 letters and ask if they know any.
activities.what_we_look_for: Whether they can hear and play with rhyming sounds, and any letter names they already know.

activities.title: Everyday play and talk
activities.instructions: Record a few minutes of ordinary play and talk together - nothing staged. This is useful context for a clinician alongside your other answers, especially if you've noticed your child losing a word, gesture or skill they used to have.
activities.what_we_look_for: A general sample of current communication and play, and any visible loss of a previously used skill.
